newsitem.title: USA: Racial murder trial of ex-U.S. soldier to begin.
newsitem.headline: Racial murder trial of ex-U.S. soldier to begin.

text.p: Jury selection will begin on Monday in the trial of the second of three white former paratroopers charged with the racially motivated shooting deaths of a black couple.

Prosecutors will seek the death penalty against Malcolm Wright, 22, who faces two counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder for the Dec. 7, 1995, killings in Fayetteville, N.C.

The trial was moved to New Hanover County Superior Court in Wilmington because of pre-trial publicity stemming from the Feb. 27 conviction of James Burmeister for the murders. Burmeister, 21, of Thompson, Pa., is serving two consecutive life sentences after a jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict on the death penalty. It deadlocked 11-1 in favour of executing him.

The murders led Army Secretary Togo West to initiate a national investigation into racist activity in military ranks. The probe found little evidence of overt racism but 22 people were subsequently discharged, including Burmeister, Wright and Randy Meadows, a third soldier charged in the crime.

Burmeister, a one-time member of Fort Bragg's elite 82nd Airborne Division, was found guilty of shooting Michael James, 36, and Jackie Burden, 27, at point blank range. Under state law he will have to serve at least 50 years before becoming eligible for parole.
Judge Coy Brewer, who also presided at the Burmeister trial, denied defence motions last week that would have prevented the death penalty from being considered in Wright's case.

Wright's lawyers, Paul Herzog and Jonathan Broun, said it would be "fundamentally unfair" for him to face the death penalty since Meadows testified that Burmeister admitted shooting James and Burden. But Assistant District Attorney Calvin Colyer, who prosecuted Burmeister, said that while the state believed Burmeister was the shooter new evidence could come to light.
"In any case, it isn't necessary to show that Wright intended specifically to kill Michael James and Jackie Burden," he said. "All we have to show is that Wright intended for them to die."

Meadows, 22, was the state's star witness in the three-week Burmeister trial and will also testify against Wright. In exchange for his testimony, two counts of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder were dropped by the prosecution and he will be sentenced in the fall on assault charges.

Meadows, of Mulkeytown, Ill. testified that Burmeister hated blacks, Jews, gays and other minorities and talked of killing a black person so he could gain a higher rank in the racist skinhead group he helped establish on the post. He also said Burmeister admired a spider web tattoo on Wright's left arm, which Wright had said was symbolic of killing a black person.

Wright, of Lexington, Ky., was compelled to show the tattoo to the Burmeister jury as part of the state's case, but Herzog has asked that Judge Brewer suppress it during Wright's trial, arguing it would prejudice jurors against his client.
Brewer denied the motion but said prosecutors would have to make a formal request to enter the tattoo into evidence.

Following his conviction, Burmeister requested protective custody at the predominantly black prison where he spends 23 hours a day alone in a cell, showering and exercising for the other hour. On March 18, a breach in security allowed an unidentified black prisoner to attack him, but prison officials said Burmeister was not seriously injured.
